title: Working With a Leader Who Is Overwhelmed
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece offers tactical advice for team members reporting to an overwhelmed leader, describing the recognizable symptoms — forgetfulness, impaired decision-making, canceled or unprepared meetings, rising impatience — and then providing a five-part playbook for managing the relationship. Recommendations include offering to take something off the leader's plate, documenting every commitment since the leader won't remember them, timing non-urgent conversations carefully, proactively updating the leader to reduce their need to ask questions, and always bringing proposed solutions rather than raw problems. The piece closes by urging team members not to let a leader's stress become contagious.
points: Catalogs recognizable symptoms of an overwhelmed leader: forgetfulness, impaired decisions, missed or unprepared meetings, rising impatience.
Recommends documenting all commitments in writing, since an overwhelmed leader is unlikely to remember what they agreed to.
Advises careful timing of non-urgent conversations, saving them for moments when the leader isn't visibly stressed.
Recommends proactive, frequent updates so the overwhelmed leader doesn't have to spend cognitive energy asking for status.
Closes with the instruction to always bring solutions rather than raw problems, and not to let the leader's stress become contagious.
quotes: Overwhelmed leaders often struggle to convey directions or priorities clearly, while also showing up late or unprepared to important meetings. Their ability to make decisions becomes impaired, while their impatience with others rises.
First, acknowledge their stress and offer to take something off their plate. The likelihood is they won’t know what to offload, but they will greatly appreciate the gesture.

Next, team members must create a paper trail for anything discussed, decided, or agreed to. Do this not to protect yourself from conflict, but because your leader won’t remember what they have committed to.
Lastly, be sure to show up with solutions, not problems. When elevating an issue, be prepared to describe what you would plan to do about it.
Don’t let their anxiety stress you out. Stay calm in the face of their impatience. Just because they are frazzled doesn’t mean you need to be.
